results.summary: This project implements a simple 32-bit RISC-V processor core with 8 general-purpose registers. It includes a boot select input, UART receive and transmit pins, and eight bidirectional GPIO pins. The design is intended to be tested over the demo board USB UART, but no test has been implemented yet. External hardware includes a boot mode selector, a UART interface, and GPIO connections.

This project is an implementation of the Izhikevich neuron model in Verilog. It accepts an 8-bit input current and outputs an 8-bit state variable. The documentation is essentially placeholder text, providing no meaningful explanation of how the design works, how to test it, or what external hardware is required. As a result, little can be said about its functionality or usage.

This design is a 3-bit up/down counter with reset, load, enable, and direction control signals. It counts on the positive clock edge when enabled, and the output can be loaded from the input data. To test it, one sets the control signals and observes the counting behavior. External hardware includes a 7-segment display with a driver and resistors to visualize the output.

This project is a ring oscillator built from a chain of 21 SkullFET inverters, producing a square wave output. It provides four output pins with the fundamental frequency and divided versions (divide-by-2, 4, and 8). The oscillator is expected to run at approximately 148.6 MHz based on simulation. Testing requires an oscilloscope connected to one of the output pins.

This is an example Verilog design intended as a template for Tiny Tapeout projects. It has two input pins and one output pin, but the documentation does not describe any specific functionality. The testing instructions are vague, and the external hardware section is left as a placeholder. The design serves as a starting point for new users.

This project implements a PQN model in Verilog that can generate Class 1 and Class 2 neuron firing patterns, selectable via a mode pin. It accepts a 12-bit input current and outputs a 16-bit membrane potential. The design was verified against Julia simulations using provided test vectors, with outputs updated every 180 clock cycles. External hardware requires only a PCB board for testing.

This project is a PWM module controlled via an SPI interface. It provides three PWM outputs and several status pins indicating non-zero register values. The SPI interface allows programming of counter and duty cycle registers, and override pins enable direct PWM testing. External hardware includes an SPI master and a way to observe the PWM signals.

This project implements RISC-V Mini, a compact 8-bit RISC-V processor core with a 16-bit compressed instruction set. It accepts a 16-bit instruction and outputs an 8-bit result, with different instruction types producing specific outputs. The design is intended for educational purposes and fits within Tiny Tapeout constraints. Testing involves setting the instruction and clocking once to receive the result.

This project is an 8-bit custom RISC processor with a Von Neumann architecture and multicycle design. It features an ALU, 16 general-purpose registers, a stack pointer, and a program counter, and communicates with external memory via an 8-bit data bus and 15-bit address bus. Testing requires connecting external memory, loading a program, and providing a clock. The design is notable for its detailed documentation and custom instruction set.

This project is a hardware driver for the Adafruit 2.13-inch e-ink display, using an SPI master to communicate with the SSD1680 chipset. It can display eight built-in patterns selected by input pins, and also supports copying SRAM contents to the display. The driver initializes the display, sends image data, and puts it into deep sleep to retain the image. External hardware includes the e-ink display and jumper wires to connect it to the PMOD.
